hook: Agents are systems that act — which means agent architecture is architecture where **a mistake becomes an action**. This reel adapts GA-30's toolkit for the agentic era: platform design, tenancy, budgets, and adoption.

scenes.title: The agent reference architecture: six layers, every production agent
scenes.sub: Gateway · orchestrator · tools · memory · guardrails · observability
scenes.narration: GA-30 gave GenAI systems five blocks; agents add agency, so the reference architecture gains a layer and sharpens three. The GATEWAY is where requests enter: authentication, rate limiting, per-tenant quotas, request normalization — everything AG-19 learned about APIs, now the agent's front door. The ORCHESTRATOR runs the loop — plan, act, observe — and it's where AG-14's control design and AG-18's human-in-the-loop checkpoints live; treat it as stateless where possible — loop state goes to memory, so orchestrator instances scale horizontally. TOOLS are the action surface: each one a scoped capability with an explicit contract, and AG-16's registry discipline — the tool list IS your attack surface. MEMORY is scoped per user/tenant with TTLs (AG-17) — and in a multi-agent org, memory stores carry ACLs just like documents do. GUARDRAILS wrap input, output, and tool calls (AG-09) — for agents the third one matters most: screen the ACTION, not just the text. And OBSERVABILITY (AG-20/21) must trace every loop iteration, every tool call, every token — an agent you can't trace is an agent you can't ship.

annot: Gateway quotas before the loop — an unauthenticated request must never reach the orchestrator
Orchestrator stateless, state in memory — horizontal scaling without sticky sessions
Guardrails have THREE surfaces for agents: input, output, and the action itself

scenes.title: Agent platform design: one platform, many agents
scenes.sub: When the second agent ships, you're not building agents — you're building a platform
scenes.narration: The first agent is a project; by the third, patterns repeat and the smart move is a PLATFORM — shared infrastructure that individual agents configure, not rebuild. The platform provides: the gateway — one front door with auth and quotas for every agent; the tool registry — tools built once, permissioned per agent (AG-16); memory stores — shared infra, tenant-scoped data (AG-17); the observability plane — one trace format across all agents (AG-20); and eval harnesses — golden sets and CI gates as a service (AG-21). Individual agents then become CONFIGURATION: which tools, which memory scopes, which guardrail policies, which budget — an agent definition file, versioned in git, reviewed like code. This is the moment build-vs-buy-configure gets real: a platform for internal productivity agents is configure-heavy — open-source framework plus your gateway and policies; but if agents ARE your product, the orchestrator and eval harness may be exactly where you build. The platform question to ask early: how does a NEW agent go from idea to production? If the answer is 'three teams and two months', you have projects, not a platform.

scenes.title: An agent definition file — an agent as configuration
scenes.body:
# agents/support-triage.yaml — versioned, reviewed, deployed like code
name: support-triage
version: 3.2.0

model: { deployment: my-gpt4o, temperature: 0.2 }

tools:                      # from the platform registry (AG-16)
  - ticket.search          { scope: read }
  - ticket.reply           { scope: draft, hitl: required }   # AG-18
  - kb.lookup              { scope: read }
  - refund.issue           { scope: none }                    # not granted

memory:                     # platform stores, agent-scoped (AG-17)
  - store: conversation     { scope: per-user, ttl: 90d }
  - store: user-profile     { scope: per-user, ttl: none, pii: masked }

guardrails:                 # platform policies + agent overrides
  input_screen:  standard
  output_screen: standard
  action_screen: strict     # screen tool ARGS, not just text (AG-09)

budget:                     # per-run guardrails (AG-23)
  max_steps: 12
  max_cost_usd: 0.35
  deadline_seconds: 240

evals:                      # CI gates (AG-21)
  golden_set: evals/triage-golden.jsonl
  min_task_success: 0.92
annot: The whole agent is data — code review, version history, and rollback come free
refund.issue with scope 'none' — the tool list is the permission model; deny by default
budget block is AG-23's circuit breaker as policy — every agent gets one before production

scenes.title: Multi-tenant concerns: the blast radius question
scenes.sub: Isolation isn't optional when one mistake hits every customer at once
scenes.narration: Multi-tenancy is where agent architecture stops being diagram work and becomes liability work. ISOLATION has three rings: DATA — every memory store, cache entry, and retrieval index carries a tenant key, enforced at the store's ACL layer, not by convention in prompts — a prompt that says 'only use this tenant's data' is not a security boundary, it's a suggestion; EXECUTION — decide per tool whether tenants share runtime or get sandboxes — a shared code-interpreter is a cross-tenant exfiltration channel (AG-22), so tenants get isolated sandboxes or the tool is read-only; and QUOTA — per-tenant budgets at the gateway — one tenant's runaway loop must starve alone (AG-23). Then COST MODELING: tenants multiply everything — cost per completed task (GA-30) becomes cost per tenant per task class, and pricing must map to the budget block: max steps, token ceilings, tool-call rates per tier. NOISY NEIGHBOR effects are agent-specific: loops amplify — a tenant with pathological inputs can burn 100x quota — so hard per-tenant circuit breakers, not alerts. And COMPLIANCE MATRIX: which tenants' data may which models see? A matrix of tenant x data-class x model-providers, maintained as code, becomes your GDPR/hipaa answer.

scenes.title: Tenant isolation — enforced in the stores, not the prompts
scenes.body:
# The rule: tenant_id is a SYSTEM field, never model-provided.

async def retrieve(query: str, tenant_id: str):
    # ACL enforced by the store's filter — unforgeable,
    # unlike a prompt instruction the model could ignore.
    return vector_store.search(
        query,
        filter={"tenant_id": tenant_id},   # ← the boundary
        top_k=8,
    )

async def run_sandboxed(code: str, tenant_id: str):
    # Shared interpreter = cross-tenant exfiltration (AG-22).
    # Per-tenant ephemeral sandbox, network egress denied.
    async with sandbox.for_tenant(tenant_id) as sb:
        return await sb.exec(code, network="deny")

# Gateway-level per-tenant circuit breaker (AG-23):
#   budget: 500 steps / 10 min sliding window
#   on breach: shed load for THAT tenant only, 503 + Retry-After
annot: filter={tenant_id} at the store layer — a prompt can be jailbroken; an ACL filter cannot
Sandbox per tenant with egress denied — the shared-interpreter lesson from AG-22, priced in
Circuit breaker sheds ONE tenant — everyone else's agents keep running

scenes.title: Adoption roadmap, risk & compliance matrix, build-buy-configure
scenes.sub: Shipping the platform is 30% — the other 70% is the org around it
scenes.narration: The ADOPTION ROADMAP runs in three horizons: PILOT — one use-case, one team, human-in-the-loop mandatory, weekly eval reviews — success is measured in trust earned, not tasks automated; EXPAND — three to five use-cases on the shared platform, first self-serve agent definitions, publish the internal catalog so teams discover instead of rebuild; and PLATFORM — agent definitions as a paved road: template, evals, guardrails, and budget pre-wired — new agents deploy in days. The RISK & COMPLIANCE MATRIX tracks: data residency per tenant, model provider approvals, action-class approvals (read-only vs write vs money-moving), audit retention — each row has an owner and an expiry review date, because compliance answers rot. Finally, sourcing: BUILD the orchestrator if agents are your product; CONFIGURE a framework plus your gateway/policies if they're internal leverage; BUY turnkey copilots for commodity tasks — and revisit the decision twice a year, because the line between 'commodity' and 'differentiator' moves fast in this field. The architect's job at this altitude is deciding what NOT to build.

scenes.title: Risk & compliance matrix — as code
scenes.body:
# compliance/tenants.yaml — reviewed quarterly, expiring answers die
- tenant: acme-corp
  residency: eu-west
  models_allowed: [azure-openai-eu, llama-selfhost]   # GDPR path
  action_classes:
    read:      auto
    write:     hitl_required                       # AG-18
    financial: forbidden
  audit_retention_days: 730
  review_by: 2026-Q1

- tenant: internal-ops
  residency: any
  models_allowed: [any-approved]
  action_classes: { read: auto, write: auto, financial: hitl_required }
  audit_retention_days: 90
  review_by: 2026-Q1

# CI check: an agent definition may only reference
# tools/models/action_classes its tenants' rows allow.
# Violations fail the build — compliance as a test, not a meeting.
annot: Action classes per tenant — 'write' auto-approved for internal ops, human-required for customers
review_by dates — stale compliance answers are worse than none; they look authoritative
Enforced in CI — the matrix is executable, so it can't drift into a spreadsheet fiction

recap: Agent reference architecture: gateway, orchestrator, tools, memory, guardrails, observability — with guardrails screening actions and the orchestrator kept stateless
By the third agent, build a platform: shared gateway, tool registry, memory stores, observability, eval harnesses — agents become versioned configuration files
Multi-tenancy: tenant keys enforced at the store ACL (never in prompts), per-tenant sandboxes, and circuit breakers that shed one tenant, not all
Adoption runs pilot → expand → platform; keep the risk & compliance matrix as code with owners and expiry dates — and revisit build-vs-buy twice a year

quiz.q: Why must tenant isolation be enforced at the vector store's ACL filter instead of via prompt instructions?
opts: A prompt instruction can be ignored or jailbroken by the model — a store-level filter is a system boundary the model cannot override
ACL filters are cheaper than prompt tokens
quiz.why: Anything in the prompt is advisory — AG-09/AG-22 showed models can be steered around instructions. Isolation must live in a layer the model has no influence over: the data store's filter, sandbox, or gateway quota.

quiz.q: What turns individual agent projects into an agent PLATFORM?
opts: Centralizing shared infrastructure — gateway, tool registry, memory stores, observability, eval harnesses — so each new agent is a versioned configuration file, not a rebuild
Moving all agents onto managed cloud services
Writing more documentation about the agents
quiz.why: The platform test: how long does a NEW agent take from idea to production? If shared layers exist and an agent is config, it's days. If every agent rebuilds auth, tools, memory, and observability, you have projects — regardless of what the org chart says.

quiz.q: For agents, guardrails gain a third screening surface beyond input and output. What is it?
opts: The tool-call arguments — the ACTION itself must be screened, because an agent's mistake is an executed action, not just harmful text
quiz.why: Text screening stops harmful content; action screening stops harmful DEEDS — refund.issue(to: attacker) is perfectly polite text. Agents need input, output, AND action screening (AG-09's boundary applied to the tool surface).

code.title: The platform contract
annot: One file per agent — reviewable, versioned, rollback-able
Deny-by-default tools — the registry grants; the definition cannot exceed
Budget + evals are pre-wired — the paved road IS the platform

notes:
# Agent Architect Toolkit — AG notes

## Reference architecture (6 layers)
Gateway (auth/quota) → Orchestrator (loop, stateless; state in memory) → Tool runtime (contracts, sandbox, audit) → Memory (scoped, TTL'd, ACL'd) · Guardrails (input + output + ACTION) · Observability (full loop tracing).

## Platform design
By agent #3, centralize: gateway, tool registry, memory infra, observability plane, eval harness. Agents become YAML definitions: model, tools, memory, guardrails, budget, evals — versioned in git, reviewed like code.

## Multi-tenancy
- Isolation rings: data (store-level ACL filter — never prompts), execution (per-tenant sandboxes, deny egress), quota (per-tenant circuit breakers).
- Noisy-neighbor math: loops amplify — hard breakers, not alerts.
- Cost model: per tenant per task class; map to budget blocks per pricing tier.
- Compliance matrix: tenant x data-class x model-provider x action-class, as code with owners and review-by dates.

## Adoption roadmap
Pilot (1 use-case, HITL, trust metrics) → Expand (3–5 use-cases, self-serve definitions, internal catalog) → Platform (paved road: template + evals + guardrails + budget).

## Build vs buy vs configure
Agents = your product → build orchestrator + evals. Internal leverage → configure framework + your gateway/policies. Commodity tasks → buy. Revisit twice a year.
